Cruising
KROO-zing
noun (Silent Generation slang)
From Dutch kruisen, to cross, to sail to and fro — first a naval word for a ship patrolling back and forth. American teenagers of the 1950s borrowed it for driving slowly up and down the main street on a Friday or Saturday night, from the drive-in at one end to the turnaround at the other, to see and be seen. The practice was common in towns across the country by the late 1950s and is now remembered as a small-town rite of that era.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In 1958, cruising meant a Saturday night loop: Main Street from the Dairy Queen to the courthouse and back, windows down, radio up, waving at the same cars you had passed ten minutes before. Nobody was going anywhere. That was the point. You went to see your friends, to show off a car, and maybe to catch a girl’s eye at the stoplight. Grandpa will admit it was mostly harmless and mostly a waste of gasoline. Scripture is not against young people enjoying their youth: "Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth" (Ecc 11:9). But the same verse ends with a sober reminder that God will bring every pleasure into judgment. Cruising raised two questions every grandchild still faces. First, who is in the car? "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed" (Pro 13:20). Second, what is the night for? Paul urges, "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16). An aimless loop can be a pleasant evening with friends, or it can be the road to trouble. The young man who wants to keep his way clean finds the answer in the Psalm: "by taking heed thereto according to thy word" (Psa 119:9). Christ is the Way, and He gives every road a destination worth driving to.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (American, 1950s; from the naval word for patrolling to and fro) for driving the main street slowly on a weekend night to see and be seen — a pleasant loop that still asks whether we are redeeming the time (Eph 5:16).

CRUISING, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) Driving slowly up and down a town’s main street for company and show; also cruising the strip, cruising the drag. "Saturday night we’d go cruising from the Dairy Queen to the courthouse and back."

Webster (1828) — CRUISE, verb intransitive [See cross.] To sail back and forth, or to rove on the ocean in search of an enemys ships for capture, or for protecting commerce; or to rove for plunder as a pirate.

Decode for families: who is in the car, and where is the night going?

Key Scripture

Ecc 11:9 — "Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thine heart, and in the sight of thine eyes: but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment."

Pro 13:20 — "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed."

1Co 15:33 — "Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners."

Eph 5:16 — "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil."

Modern Corruption

Mostly innocent fun, but cruising could breed idleness, show, and bad company, which Scripture warns will corrupt good manners.

expand to see more

Cruising was the social network of 1958: a loop where young people gathered to see who was there and to be seen. Most nights it amounted to a tank of gas and a lot of waving. Youth has its proper joys, and Scripture permits them (Ecc 11:9).

The trouble came from aimlessness. A carload of bored boys with nowhere to go found mischief, drink, and fights, and the girl who climbed into the wrong car found worse. Scripture’s word to every young driver and rider is the same: choose your companions (Pro 13:20), remember that evil communications corrupt good manners (1Co 15:33), and spend your hours as a steward who must give account (Eph 5:16).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Dutch kruisen (to cross, to sail to and fro) → English cruise (17th c., naval patrol) → 1950s teen cruising the main drag → nostalgic word for the Saturday-night loop.

Dutch kruisen — to cross, from kruis, cross

17th c. English cruise — to sail to and fro on patrol

1950s American teen slang: cruising the strip or the drag

Later: nostalgic name for the small-town Saturday-night loop

Usage

""We spent half of 1958 cruising Main Street, and I don’t think we ever went anywhere.""
